prompt:
Read the transcript, then (a) summarise the call, (b) identify the root cause of the customer's problem, and (c) calculate the exact refund the customer is owed under the policy below. Show your reasoning.

Policy: Broadband outages longer than 24 continuous hours are credited at the daily rate (monthly plan / 30) per full day of outage. Partial days are not credited. If the customer was also charged a technician visit fee for a fault that turned out to be on the provider's side, that fee (₹350) is refunded in full.

Transcript:
Agent: SkyNet Broadband, how can I help?
Customer: My internet was completely down from Monday 9 am to Thursday 3 pm. I pay ₹1,200 a month for the 200 Mbps plan. I also got charged ₹350 for a technician visit on Tuesday, and the guy said the fibre was cut at your junction box, not inside my flat.
Agent: I'm sorry. Let me check... yes, the ticket says fibre cut at the street junction box, fixed Thursday 3 pm. The technician fee was auto-applied because the visit was booked under 'customer premises'.
Customer: So what do I get back?
Agent: Let me calculate that and apply the credit to your next bill.
Customer: Also please make sure this doesn't happen again, this is the second time this year.
Agent: Noted. I'll raise a request to inspect the junction box.
reference_or_rubric: (a) Summary: outage Mon 9am to Thu 3pm, customer on ₹1,200/month plan, charged ₹350 technician fee, fault was at provider's junction box, credit to next bill, customer asks for prevention; agent raises junction box inspection. (b) Root cause: fibre cut at provider's street junction box, and the visit fee was wrongly auto-applied because the visit was booked as 'customer premises'. (c) Refund: outage = 3 days 6 hours -> 3 full days x (1200/30 = ₹40) = ₹120 credit, plus ₹350 technician fee refunded = ₹470 total. Full marks require ₹470 with the 3-day (not 4-day) logic.

prompt:
Extract the termination, notice-period and liability clauses from this agreement into JSON (clause_id, topic, text). Then analyse whether any two clauses contradict each other and explain the legal implication for the Vendor.

7.1 Either party may terminate this Agreement for convenience with 60 days' written notice.
7.2 The Customer may terminate immediately upon a material breach by the Vendor that is not cured within 15 days of notice.
9.1 The Vendor's aggregate liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the fees paid in the 12 months preceding the claim.
9.2 Notwithstanding clause 9.1, the Vendor shall be liable for all losses, without limit, arising from any breach of its data-protection obligations.
12.4 The Vendor shall not be liable for any indirect or consequential loss, including loss of data, under any circumstances.
reference_or_rubric: JSON lists 7.1 (termination for convenience, 60 days), 7.2 (termination for uncured material breach, 15-day cure), 9.1 (liability cap = 12 months' fees), 9.2 (unlimited liability for data-protection breaches), 12.4 (no liability for indirect/consequential loss incl. loss of data). Contradiction: 9.2 makes Vendor liable without limit for data-protection breaches, while 12.4 excludes liability for loss of data 'under any circumstances'; these conflict when a data-protection breach causes data loss. Implication: ambiguity is likely construed against the drafter / specific (9.2 'notwithstanding') may override general (12.4); Vendor faces uncertain, potentially uncapped exposure and should reconcile the clauses. Full marks require spotting the 9.2 vs 12.4 conflict and explaining the exposure.
